standard.title: Movement strategies
standard.description: apply and adapt movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have investigated different ways of moving and manipulating objects and space and drawn conclusions about their effectiveness (AC9HP2M02). They can experiment with movement but have not yet applied structured strategies to game contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students apply and adapt movement strategies to achieve movement outcomes across a range of activity types.

nodes.label: Planning strategies in minor and small-sided games
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan and perform strategies to be successful in minor and small-sided games.
nodes.minimum_width: Plan and perform a simple movement strategy in one minor or small-sided game (e.g. a tag game, target game or net/court game) and reflect on whether it achieved the intended outcome.
nodes.typical_width: Plan and perform strategies in a range of minor and small-sided game types, reflecting on what worked and adjusting approach across games.
wider: Compare strategies across two different game categories (e.g. tag game vs target game) and explain why the same strategy does or does not transfer.
Lead a small group in planning and trialling a strategy, gathering peer feedback on its effectiveness.
nodes.hinge_reason: Planning a strategy — even a simple one — is the prerequisite cognitive move for all subsequent adaptation work. Students who act purely reactively without planning cannot access the evaluation and adaptation demands in the next nodes.

response_modes.reason: Students need a scaffold for thinking before and after a strategy attempt: what are we trying to achieve, what will we do, what happened. Brief structured reflection (e.g. a verbal debrief format) is more useful at this stage than extended written analysis.

success_criteria: Describes a strategy they will use before participating in a game.
Performs the game using the planned strategy.
Reflects on whether the strategy achieved the intended outcome.

nodes.label: Adapting strategies to create scoring opportunities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate how movement strategies can be adapted to create scoring opportunities across different game categories.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate one adapted strategy in a game context where scoring is involved, explaining what was changed and why.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate adapted strategies across invasion, target, net/court, and striking/fielding game contexts, identifying how each game's rules and structure require different adaptations.
wider: Design a new rule or constraint variation for a known game and trial it, explaining how the change shifts the strategy space for players.
Investigate how professional or community teams adapt game strategies in response to opposition — using video or direct observation — and apply one observed adaptation to their own game.

response_modes.reason: Strategy adaptation is highly context-dependent — what works in an invasion game fails in a target game. Students need exposure across game categories to build genuine strategic flexibility rather than context-specific habits.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Game category diversity (invasion, target, net/court, striking/fielding) provides a genuinely rich context space — wider students who explore strategies across all four categories develop substantially more transferable tactical understanding.
success_criteria: Identifies a scoring opportunity in a game and names a strategy to exploit it.
Adapts their movement strategy in response to a change in the game (e.g. opponent movement, rule change, new target).
Explains what they changed in their strategy and the reason for the change.

nodes.label: Centre of gravity and stability
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can manipulate their centre of gravity to enhance stability and explain how centre of gravity and base of support influence stability.
nodes.minimum_width: Perform a balance activity that requires manipulating centre of gravity; explain in simple terms how centre of gravity affects stability.
nodes.typical_width: Perform and explain centre of gravity and base of support relationships across a range of balance activities; apply this understanding deliberately when attempting unfamiliar balances.
wider: Investigate how martial arts, gymnastics, or dance practitioners deliberately use centre of gravity manipulation as a movement strategy and demonstrate one application.
Design a balance challenge for a peer that deliberately varies the base of support and centre of gravity demands, and coach them using the relevant language.

response_modes.reason: The conceptual link between centre of gravity, base of support and stability is not intuitive. Students benefit from structured vocabulary scaffolding — label-then-demonstrate rather than demonstrate-then-label — to anchor the understanding to their physical experience.

success_criteria: Demonstrates a balance that requires adjusting centre of gravity.
Identifies their base of support in the balance and explains how changing it affects stability.
Uses the terms 'centre of gravity' and 'base of support' correctly in a short explanation.

nodes.label: Evaluating game tactics
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the outcome of a game tactic that has been adapted to improve scoring options using set criteria.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a provided set of criteria to evaluate one adapted game tactic, identifying whether it improved scoring options and one change they would make.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate adapted game tactics across two or more game types using criteria, identifying strengths and areas for improvement and connecting evaluation to future strategy decisions.
wider: Develop their own evaluation criteria for assessing a game tactic, trial the criteria with peers, and refine the criteria based on what they found most useful.
Compare tactic evaluations across two game sessions to track whether strategic decision-making improved over time and explain what evidence supports this.
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluation using criteria is the capability move that connects strategy use to learning — without it, students simply repeat tactics rather than developing strategic thinking. This evaluation habit is directly required in AC9HP6M02 and underpins the more sophisticated tactical analysis expected at Y5-6.

response_modes.reason: Criteria-based evaluation is a new metacognitive layer for this age group. Providing a structured debrief format (what did we try, what happened, what would we change) and gradually releasing criteria construction to students builds the evaluation capability systematically.

success_criteria: Uses provided criteria to assess whether an adapted tactic achieved its intended effect.
Identifies at least one strength and one limitation of the tactic.
Proposes a specific change to the tactic based on their evaluation.
